blocks.text: AI-Based Platform to Support the Employment of Astana IT University Graduates.

Problem statement. Graduates need to compare their educational and practical experience with heterogeneous IT job requirements and identify an actionable next step. The existence and scale of this need specifically among AITU graduates remain hypotheses until local user discussions are completed. Research on skill extraction supports the technical relevance of the task, but does not establish local demand [S01–S05].

Target users are senior AITU students and graduates, plus an administrator of the educational prototype. A career-center representative is a potential requirements expert. An employer dashboard is outside the current MVP.

Aim. Develop and evaluate a reproducible prototype that explains how a graduate profile covers IT vacancy skill requirements, identifies skill gaps and suggests development actions. The matching percentage is not a probability of employment.

rows: At least 12 meaningfully used sources including eight scientific publications; comparison of four systems. Optional user research is planned for later validation.
A priority, acceptance criterion and verification method for each mandatory requirement.
System context, use cases, components, data relationships and API responsibilities.
Profile → skills → vacancy → explained match → development actions.
Compare exact matching, normalization and optional semantics under one fixed protocol.
Unified report, editable diagrams, traceable tasks and actual verification evidence.

blocks.text: Included: authentication and graduate/admin roles; AITU-oriented profiles and education; skills with proficiency levels; projects, certificates and experience; vacancies and saved jobs; transparent weighted matching; saved analyses with staleness detection; recommendations and administration. The local seed contains 30 fictional vacancies clearly identified as demonstration data.

Excluded from this stage: automated hiring decisions, validated prediction of employment, university SSO/DU/Moodle integration, large-scale collection of external vacancies, production SLA, employer accounts and training a large language model. Visual similarity to university services does not imply integration or institutional endorsement.
The team consists of two students. Confirmed names and GitHub accounts are recorded below. Actual contributions are recorded when supported by completed work and review evidence.

sections.title: 2. Evidence of Relevance and Optional User Research

blocks.text: On 24 October 2026, the team clarified that user interviews and supervisor feedback are optional for this submission. This is a team-reported requirement clarification, not a recorded supervisor approval.

Relevance at this stage is supported by the literature and system comparison in Sections 3–4. No user interviews were conducted and no interview results are presented. Local demand, explanation usefulness and the employment-readiness indicator remain hypotheses rather than empirically established conclusions.

blocks.text: Future optional research may include anonymized discussions with graduates, career-center staff and recruiters. Findings should be recorded with actual dates and consent, separated from interpretations and linked to requirement decisions. Such evidence is not a prerequisite for this submission and no participant identities or fabricated responses are included.

A targeted engineering search was performed on 19 October 2026 using ACL Anthology, arXiv and official product/technical documentation. Queries covered skill extraction from job postings, multilingual skill matching, sentence embeddings and job-title representations. Inclusion required verifiable metadata and a direct connection to extraction, retrieval or an engineering decision. This is not claimed to be an exhaustive systematic review.

The review uses 17 sources: eight peer-reviewed scientific publications S01–S08, technical report S09 and eight official materials S10–S17. The scientific core is from 2021–2025; Sentence-BERT (2019) is retained as foundational work. The limitations and applications below are the project’s analysis of transferability, not verbatim author claims.

blocks.text: Synthesis and research questions

S01–S04 motivate separating a skill mention, its canonical label and evidence of proficiency. The MVP therefore distinguishes an explicitly reported skill/level from inferred text evidence. Dictionary matching is reproducible but limited by catalog coverage and language variation. S03 and S05 motivate taxonomy alignment without establishing a need for a graph database at this scale.

S06 highlights information in vacancy descriptions beyond skill lists. The current score consequently measures only coverage of explicit or extracted skill requirements. S07–S09 justify evaluating embeddings against literal matching, but textual proximity alone does not establish competence. Semantic evidence is therefore capped at a partial contribution and its method is recorded.

RQ1: do alias normalization and optional semantic matching improve nDCG@5 over exact skill matching on a fixed profile/vacancy dataset while retaining interpretable explanations? RQ2: do users distinguish skill coverage from the probability of employment? The contribution is a testable engineering adaptation to AITU. Superiority over commercial systems is not asserted.

Four relevant systems are compared on eight consistent criteria using official public documentation: LinkedIn [S11], Handshake [S12], hh.kz [S13] and Coursera Career Academy [S14]. No private product accounts were audited. “Not established” means that the cited sources do not establish the capability; it does not mean the capability is absent.

blocks.text: Matching and skill-development recommendations already exist in competing systems. The rationale for this prototype is controllable AITU-specific adaptation, an accessible per-requirement calculation and reproducible evaluation on a fixed dataset. Optional future user research can test the local-demand hypothesis. Commercial systems are not quantitative baselines because their internal algorithms and evaluation data are unavailable.

The alternatives are assessed for a small educational prototype with a Python analysis module, relational data and no interaction history. Assessments are qualitative; no unperformed performance measurements are implied.

rows: FastAPI: validation/OpenAPI and direct Python NLP integration [S15]. Django REST: mature conventions and administration, with a larger framework surface. Node.js/NestJS: a shared frontend language, but Python NLP needs an additional integration boundary.
FastAPI supports one small API/analysis process and a modular code structure.

PostgreSQL: relational constraints and transactions [S16]. SQLite: simple setup with a different concurrency/operation profile. MongoDB: flexible documents, with a different strategy for cross-record integrity.
PostgreSQL with SQLAlchemy and Alembic preserves linked profiles, catalog entries and vacancy requirements.

Exact matching: transparent but sensitive to wording. Dictionary/aliases/weights: explainable but requires catalog maintenance. Embedding hybrid: supports paraphrases [S07–S09] but adds calibration and inference cost.
Weighted normalized keyword matching is the default; embeddings remain optional and require separate evaluation.

REST/JSON: straightforward CRUD and OpenAPI. GraphQL: flexible selections with an additional schema/cost-control layer. gRPC: typed binary communication but more integration work for a browser client.
REST/JSON under /api, with Vite/nginx proxying to a single browser origin.

React/TypeScript: typed components already implemented. Vue/TypeScript: a comparable SPA option requiring component migration. Server templates: a smaller client stack but a different approach to interactive profile editing.
React/TypeScript with Vite follows the implemented journeys; no unmeasured speed advantage is claimed.

blocks.text: ADR-01: use a modular monolith. Authorization, API, analysis and persistence have separate code responsibilities but share one backend deployment. Revisit separation only if profiling demonstrates interference from inference. ADR-02: PostgreSQL is the source of truth; preserve algorithm version and input revisions with saved analyses. ADR-03: absence of the optional model must not break keyword analysis.

MoSCoW priorities: Must denotes mandatory MVP behavior; Should denotes a planned improvement; Could denotes an optional extension. An implemented feature is not evidence that users need it. Requirement IDs connect the specification, components, tasks and verification.

blocks.text: Matching and readiness rules

Score = 100 × Σ(weight × contribution) / Σ(weight). For an explicit skill, contribution = min(1, user_level / required_level); for an absent skill it is zero. Inferred text and semantic evidence are capped at 0.5. Required/preferred skill weights default to 2/1 and may be set to other positive values. Scores across different vacancies do not imply equal job difficulty.

Readiness is an internal heuristic: market 60%, projects 15%, experience 10%, certificates 5% and education 10%, with configurable normalized weights. Market uses up to five highest-scoring target-role vacancies; relevant experience is capped at 180 non-overlapping days. These weights have not been empirically validated as predictors of employment.
AI functionality: implemented baseline and optional learned extension

The implemented decision-support baseline is deterministic: it extracts known skill terms and aliases, combines profile evidence, scores vacancy requirements and derives gap-based actions. This is a knowledge-based matching pipeline, not a trained employment predictor or a generative assistant. The learned AI extension is a local sentence-embedding adapter; it is disabled in the verified configuration. The report therefore separates working rule-based functionality from available but unevaluated machine-learning functionality.

blocks.text: Illustrative calculation, not a real student result: Python level 3 of required 3 with weight 2 contributes 2; SQL level 1 of required 2 with weight 2 contributes 1; absent Git with weight 1 contributes 0. The score is 100 × (2 + 1 + 0) / (2 + 2 + 1) = 60%. Python is matched, SQL is partial and Git is missing. This demonstrates an explainable calculation, not measured recommendation accuracy.

Implementation reference: https://github.com/vbl0-0/AITU-Career/blob/prob-period-1/backend/app/ai/matching.py. Matching correctness tests verify rules and boundaries. Only an independent relevance experiment can establish whether this approach ranks useful vacancies better than simpler alternatives.

Students/graduates and administrators use React, FastAPI and PostgreSQL. University SSO and DU/Moodle are not integrated. Default keyword analysis needs no external AI service; the optional embedding model is disabled in the verified configuration.

blocks.text: Operational evaluation protocol in response to SUP-01 and SUP-02

The following is a next-stage protocol, not a completed experiment. Freeze 20 anonymized or synthetic profiles and 50 legally usable vacancies, using at least five candidates per evaluated profile. Use ten profiles for development and ten held-out profiles for testing; store IDs, source permissions, split membership and data hashes. This produces 500 development and 500 held-out profile–vacancy pairs. Where development and test share vacancies, the stated claim concerns new profiles rather than unseen vacancies.

blocks.text: Two raters independent of the matching implementation should assign relevance grades 0 (irrelevant), 1 (partly relevant) and 2 (suitable), without seeing algorithm scores. Store both original ratings and weighted Cohen's kappa before adjudication. Rater identities and actual dates remain unfilled until the work occurs. Tune aliases and semantic thresholds only on development data; use the same eligible candidates for all methods and break score ties by vacancy ID.

rows: Precision@5 = count of grade-2 vacancies in the first five / 5. nDCG@5 uses gains 2^grade − 1 and log2(rank + 1) discount, normalized by the ideal top-five ranking.
Macro-average per held-out profile. Profiles with zero ideal gain have undefined nDCG and are counted separately; report their number and candidate coverage. Preserve per-profile rankings and labels.
Micro precision, recall and F1 against annotated canonical skill mentions; show separate Kazakh/Russian/English results and representative errors.
Keep span/skill reference annotations and the exact normalization rules. No extraction-accuracy figure is currently claimed.
Same CPU, RAM, data, process and cache conditions; 30 warm-up requests, then 200 measured requests. Record median and p95, model loading separately, and errors.
Keyword p95 target is at most 500 ms. Pre-register a separate semantic latency/memory budget before comparing B2. Preserve request timings and environment details.
Use seed 42 and 1,000 paired profile-level bootstrap resamples for the nDCG difference; report a 95% interval and Precision@5 changes.

Adopt an extension only if held-out nDCG improves with an interval above zero, Precision@5 does not deteriorate, its registered resource budget is met and functional regressions are absent. Otherwise retain the simpler method and report the negative outcome.

blocks.text: Execution responsibilities are planned: Zhan coordinates the dataset, annotation records and error analysis; Ayadil prepares the reproducible B0/B1/B2 runner, model/configuration hashes and latency measurements. Both inspect the held-out results and review each other's experiment changes. Independent raters must be recruited; account ownership or an AI-assisted check is not treated as expert relevance annotation. The tracker schedules label preparation in #10 and baseline/latency evaluation in #11 for the next stage.

Expected evaluation artifacts: a dataset/split manifest, independent labels and agreement record, a committed comparison runner, environment/model configuration, per-profile rankings, metrics/timing files and an interpretation of errors and negative results. These artifacts are planned and are not listed as already available. The 60 backend and 20 browser tests establish implementation behavior, not AI effectiveness.

Validity threats include convenience sampling, self-reported skills, synthetic vacancies, language bias, tuning leakage, facilitator effects and a small profile sample. Mitigations are independent annotation, a held-out split, negative examples, fixed comparison conditions and retention of raw judgments and errors. Docker and the real embedding model were not exercised in this environment; controlled tests do not replace their evaluation.

Responsibilities below are supported by dated account-linked delivery records. OpenAI Codex assisted implementation, packaging, technical verification and publication. These records establish what was delivered under each account; imported history alone does not establish exclusive original authorship or the time each person spent. Actual human peer review remains to be added in GitHub, as requested by the supervisor.
